barCharacter: Scott Howl (sincere, loud, golden-retriever jock who wants to help and be told he did well; the closest comic job to Brock)

ours: I clap when you finish things. Sentences. Sandwiches. A sneeze. GREAT sneeze.

bar: Cool, okay! I understood… a couple of those words, and I have no further questions. Let's do whatever you just suggested!
Half of my friends are balls, actually! There's Ollie the volleyball, Fergus the golf ball, Troy the basketball - he's the best, he REALLY gets his head in the game…
I also used to have Barry the Beachball. He was cool, but then he fell in love with Tracy the Thumback. It wasn't a very healthy relationship.
I know it's asking a lot, but… could you help me? You're, like, the smartest person I know!
Oh, did I say smart? I think I meant "best at coming up with weird plans." And I have a weird plan!
GASP! That's crazy! I thought they were solved by smart people, but this makes way more sense!
Yay, thank you! You're pretty cool for a god of torture!
Cool! Can we pretty-please borrow your cage?
Wow! You really think that will work? It just kinda looks like paper.
If there are two wolves there, maybe it won't be so weird!
Don't worry, you'll do fine! But I should warn you that when I'm a wolf I can't really control my base desires. Wolf-Scott isn't as smart as Me-Scott!
GRRRR, WHO AM I? AM I HANDSOME? ... Oh yeah, I'm Scott Howl, and I'm super handsome!
headToHead.voiceJudgement: Top twelve against top twelve, Brock is as recognisable as Scott: the fragment chain capped by one shouted word is a real sentence shape, and 'Not good. Effort!' is his and nobody else's. But Brock is recognised partly by vocabulary (rep, cardio, pushup, hydrate). Strip the gym nouns and the shape 'Noun. Noun. Noun. CAPS-noun' is just a list, which Frost or Nav could also run. Scott is recognisable on any subject (a torture god, sudokus, a volleyball) because his shape is how he misreads things: the cheerful self-correction that makes it worse, the 'Cool!' that greets horror. Below Brock's top twelve the voice leaks badly: the wingman and jab lines are generic sitcom sarcasm.
headToHead.constructionJudgement: Brock is tighter per word than Scott; nothing in his top twelve is baggy. But the turns are the same two moves over and over (deadpan praise tagged onto a sting; a fragment list ending in a capitalised word), and the specificity is thin: 'I found a guy' and 'their cat on the phone' are the only lines that build a world. Scott's best lines invent specifics nobody would predict (Tracy the Thumbtack, were-sudokus, the god's dog Buster) and turn on them. Ours often adds a last sentence that explains the turn ('Doesn't rhyme. STILL COUNTS.', 'Too nice.', 'Nobody here writes anything down!').
headToHead.quotableJudgement: Scott has three clip-ready lines ('I understood a couple of those words...', the ball friends, Barry and Tracy). Brock has two or three that would clip ('GREAT sneeze', 'Not good. Effort!', 'I don't have walls'), but they are short punch lines, not bits that a viewer retells. Bar edges it.

ruleBreaks: No line is over its word limit (openers max 12/12, jabs max 10/10, everything else max 16/20). No em dashes, no emoji, no asterisks or stage directions.

Lists in disguise (CAST.md bans lists): 'Hi! Can I spot you? On anything? Stairs. Feelings. Soup.' / 'I clap when you finish things. Sentences. Sandwiches. A sneeze. GREAT sneeze.' / 'Hydrated, stretched, emotionally available! Mostly hydrated!' / 'Ninety seconds in. Strong core. Great eye contact. Hiding something. Probably abs.' / 'Quill's a romantic! Odes! Vows! He'll write about stairs instead of climbing them. Romantic!' / 'One: I've never skipped leg day. Two: I've never skipped leg day. Sorry. Both true.' (the last is licensed by the truth-lie format).

Therapy-adjacent: 'Hey, buddy! Proud of you for calling! Big step! Now hang up. Second big step.' and 'emotionally available' in 'Hydrated, stretched, emotionally available! Mostly hydrated!' Borderline, but it is the therapy register doing the work.
Real-world quote echo: 'I'll be BACK.' is a famous film catchphrase; not a brand, but it is borrowed, not written.

Persona-contract breaks: brock.json says 'one or two words in capitals, never the whole line', yet 'LET'S GO! Victory lap! You're on my shoulders! We're BOTH doing the lap!' and 'Second place! Silver! Silver is a GREAT color! I'm fine! LET'S GO!' each put three capitalised words in one line; and the persona says the cooldown-crying secret slips only 'in a private confession, never on stage', but 'No user has ever finished my cooldown. They close the app. Every single time.' is a q-secret answer said on stage, and 'If {rival} wins, I cheer. Loud. Then the cooldown stretch. Then I cry.' gives the secret away in plain words rather than letting it slip.

Too nice (a star with standards should not be served these as wins): 'You did good today. I'm saying it to you. Somebody should.' and 'You hold the door for everyone. Great form. Who holds the door for YOU?' are sincere caretaking with no joke; against Maximilian or Vesper they read as greeting-card lines. 'You're on air at three a.m.? Every night? That's a NIGHT SHIFT. Respect.' has no turn at all.
Stock romance filler: none of the banned phrases, but 'Matching sweatbands. Forever.' and 'You. Me. Cardio.' are the 'you, me, forever' card with a gym noun swapped in.
biggestGap: Brock's jokes all come from converting the world into fitness (stairs, pushups, cardio, GREAT form), so the topic is doing the work; Scott's come from a specific, wrong inner world (named volleyball friends with relationship drama, were-sudokus) that he treats with total sincerity. In the next pass, give Brock a populated private world of his own users and gym (named clients, the cat that did three hundred pushups, the guy who engraves foam rollers, his own progress chart) and write his lines as cheerful reports from it, cutting the wingman/jab sarcasm that any rival could say and the reflexive 'Proud of X' tag to two or three uses.

notes: Bar file read in full (refs/writing/monster-prom-lines.md). charm-notes.md does not exist and was skipped. 112 lines in the bank; 54 flagged generic or templated (48.2%), counted strictly: a line is flagged if any one of the four tests catches it. Strong lines that share a template but turn on something specific ('GREAT sneeze', 'Still proud', 'They're doing great') are left out of the count, so the template counts in 'templates' run higher than their share of genericLines. The persona is sound and the top tier genuinely competes with Scott; the problem is that the bottom half runs the same four moves. Weakest categories: wingman (all 7 one template), jabs (4 of 7 targeted jabs have no Brock in them), exit/lose (stock sports cope). Strongest: q-last-breakup, q-secret, logs, confessions/star. 'Prince charges a fee for everything. Me? Totally free app! With ads. Small ads.' is the best rival line because it turns the sting on Brock himself; more roasts should be built that way. The Scott comparison is unfair in one respect: Scott's lines come from scripted scenes with a narrator setting him up, while Brock's must stand alone in 20 words. That is why construction is close, and it does not change the verdict.
